hypothesis: The neuron responds strongly to extended, high-contrast linear structures oriented horizontally or diagonally, typically manifesting as sharp boundaries, shadow gaps, or distinct bands dividing the visual field. The activating feature is consistently a long, continuous edge or strip—such as a dark shadow crevice between objects, a bright metallic highlight, the silhouette of a boat hull or insect body, or a graphical dividing line—that creates a stark luminance transition (e.g., light-to-dark or light-dark-light) against the surrounding area. The neuron is invariant to object identity (firing for insects, boats, architecture, and electronics alike), texture, and lighting direction, provided the strong linear geometry and high luminance contrast are present. The activating linear feature typically spans 70–100% of the image width while occupying only 5–20% of the vertical height, usually positioned centrally or bisecting the frame. The dominant tones are neutral, featuring deep blacks, dark charcoals, and bright whites or silvers, set against variable monochromatic backgrounds of medium to light grey.
